Yes. In fact, if you want GitHub Copilot to generate code consistently and follow architectural rules, **a specification file is one of the best approaches**.

There are several levels of effectiveness:

## 1. Use a `copilot-instructions.md` file (Recommended)

GitHub Copilot supports repository-level custom instructions.

Create:

.github/copilot-instructions.md

Example:

# Project Architecture  

  

This project follows Clean Architecture.  

  

Rules:  

- Controllers must not use repositories directly.  

- All business logic goes through Application Services.  

- Dependency Injection is mandatory.  

- Use async/await everywhere.  

- Do not use static classes except for constants.  

- Logging must use ILogger<T>.  

- Use Result<T> instead of throwing exceptions for business validations.  

  

Database:  

- PostgreSQL  

- Entity Framework Core  

  

Testing:  

- xUnit  

- FluentAssertions  

  

Code Style:  

- File-scoped namespaces  

- Primary constructors when possible  

- Use var only when type is obvious

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Copilot will automatically use these instructions as additional context.

---

## 2. Create Architecture Decision Records (ADR)

Copilot is surprisingly good at reading ADRs when they're close to the code.

Example:

/docs/adr/  

├── 001-event-driven.md  

├── 002-postgresql.md  

├── 003-outbox-pattern.md

Example:

# ADR-003 Outbox Pattern  

  

Status: Accepted  

  

Context:  

Messages must never be lost.  

  

Decision:  

All integrations use the Outbox Pattern.  

  

Consequences:  

- No direct publish after SaveChanges().  

- Message records are persisted first.  

- Dispatcher publishes asynchronously.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

When generating new code, Copilot often follows these decisions.

---

## 3. Add a Project Blueprint

I use this a lot with AI tools.

Example:

/docs/project-blueprint.md

# Layers  

  

## Api  

Only HTTP endpoints.  

  

## Application  

Use cases and orchestration.  

  

## Domain  

Entities and business rules.  

  

## Infrastructure  

External implementations.  

  

# Message Bus  

  

Commands:  

command.sales.*  

  

Events:  

event.sales.*  

  

# Dependency Flow  

  

Api  

-> Application  

-> Domain  

  

Infrastructure implements ports only.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Then, in Copilot Chat:

Read docs/project-blueprint.md and create a new Sales module.

The results are usually much more accurate.

---

## 4. Use Prompt Files for Complex Features

Create:

/specs/

Example:

specs/create-customer.md

Feature: Create Customer  

  

Requirements:  

- Customer must have Name and Email.  

- Email must be unique.  

- Validation in Application layer.  

- Repository interface in Domain.  

- EF implementation in Infrastructure.  

- Publish event.customer.created.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Then ask:

Implement specs/create-customer.md.

This is very close to what Cursor, Claude Code, and Copilot Agent workflows do internally.

---

## 5. Use `.github/issues` as Specifications

A surprisingly effective workflow:

Title:  

Implement Inventory Reservation  

  

Requirements:  

- Reserve stock.  

- Reject if insufficient quantity.  

- Publish event.inventory.reserved.  

- Support idempotency.  

  

Acceptance Criteria:  

- Unit tests pass.  

- Integration tests pass.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Then:

Implement issue #123

Copilot Agent can use the issue as the source of truth.

---

## 6. For Large Projects: Create an AI Context Folder

A structure I recommend:

/docs/ai/  

├── architecture.md  

├── coding-standards.md  

├── messaging.md  

├── database.md  

├── naming-conventions.md  

└── examples/

Example:

docs/ai/

Naming Convention  

  

Commands:  

command.{bounded-context}.{action}  

  

Examples:  

command.sales.create-order  

command.inventory.reserve-stock  

  

Events:  

event.{bounded-context}.{event-name}  

  

Examples:  

event.sales.order-created  

event.inventory.stock-reserved

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Then start prompts with:

Read the files under docs/ai and create a new Billing module.

---

## 7. Best Practice with Copilot Agent Mode

If you're using the newer Copilot Agent experience, give it:

1. Architecture document  

2. Coding standards  

3. Feature specification  

4. Acceptance criteria  

5. Example implementation

AI performs much better when given:

Rule + Example + Acceptance Criteria

than only:

Rule

For example:

Rule:  

All commands must be implemented as Wolverine handlers.  

  

Example:  

Features/Sales/CreateOrderHandler.cs  

  

Acceptance Criteria:  

- Uses Wolverine.  

- Uses ILogger.  

- Uses repository abstraction.  

- Publishes event.sales.order-created.  

- Contains unit tests.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

This produces far more consistent results than a simple prompt.

For your style of development (modular monolith, Wolverine, NATS, Clean Architecture), I'd create:

.github/copilot-instructions.md  

docs/ai/architecture.md  

docs/ai/messaging.md  

docs/ai/examples/  

`

and keep a complete example module (`Sales`) that Copilot can imitate. AI models are much better at **following an existing example** than at interpreting abstract architectural rules.


Yes. The biggest problem with specs is not creating them, it's **making sure the code continues to respect them months later**.

The best approach is to make the spec **executable** and **verifiable**, not just documentation.

## 1. Link Spec to User Stories / Features

Instead of:

docs/specs/create-order.md

Use:

specs/  

├── ORD-001-create-order.md  

├── INV-002-reserve-stock.md

Include an ID:

# ORD-001 Create Order  

  

Requirements  

- Validate customer exists.  

- Save order.  

- Publish event.sales.order-created.  

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Then reference the ID in code:

/// Implements ORD-001  

public sealed class CreateOrderHandler  

{  

}

and commits:

feat(ORD-001): implement order creation

Now you can trace:

Spec -> Commit -> Code

---

## 2. Convert Requirements into Tests

This is the most effective solution.

Spec:

ORD-001  

- Customer must exist.  

- Event must be published.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Tests:

[Fact]  

public async Task Should_fail_when_customer_does_not_exist()  

{  

}  

  

[Fact]  

public async Task Should_publish_order_created_event()  

{  

}  

`

If someone changes the code incorrectly later:

Spec -> Test fails -> Developer fixes

The tests become the living specification.

---

## 3. Architecture Tests

For Clean Architecture, use tools such as:

NetArchTest  

ArchUnitNET

Example:

[Fact]  

public void Controllers_must_not_reference_infrastructure()  

{  

Types.InAssembly(ApiAssembly)  

.That()  

.ResideInNamespace("*.Controllers")  

.ShouldNot()  

.HaveDependencyOn("Infrastructure")  

.GetResult()  

.IsSuccessful  

.Should()  

.BeTrue();  

}

Now your architecture rules become executable.

If somebody violates the spec:

Controller -> Repository

the build fails.

---

## 4. Add Spec References in Code

Example:

// Spec: ORD-001  

public sealed record CreateOrderCommand(  

Guid CustomerId,  

decimal Amount);

or

/// Spec: INV-002  

public sealed class ReserveStockHandler  

{  

}

A simple search for:

ORD-001

shows everything related to that requirement.

---

## 5. Create a CI Validation Step

A PR should answer:

## Specification  

  

ORD-001  

  

## Acceptance Criteria  

  

- [x] Customer validated  

- [x] Event published  

- [x] Tests added

![](data:image/png;base64,)

GitHub Actions can even require the field.

---

## 6. Use Specification-by-Example

Instead of writing:

Reserve inventory.

![](data:image/png;base64,)

Write:

Scenario: Successful reservation  

  

Given stock = 10  

When reserve 5  

Then remaining stock = 5  

  

Scenario: Insufficient inventory  

  

Given stock = 3  

When reserve 5  

Then operation fails  

``

Then implement those examples as tests.

This is very close to BDD and greatly reduces ambiguity.

---

## 7. Add Examples Copilot Can Reuse

This is extremely important.

If you have:

Sales/  

CreateOrderHandler.cs  

CreateOrderTests.cs  

CreateOrderSpec.md

then when creating:

Billing/  

CreateInvoiceHandler.cs

Copilot will often replicate the same structure.

AI follows patterns better than rules.

---

## 8. My Preferred Setup

For a modular monolith with Wolverine/NATS:

/specs  

ORD-001-create-order.md  

  

/src  

Sales  

CreateOrderHandler.cs  

CreateOrderTests.cs  

  

/tests  

ArchitectureTests.cs  

  

/.github  

copilot-instructions.md

Where:

- **Specs** define requirements.
- **Unit tests** enforce behavior.
- **Architecture tests** enforce design.
- **Copilot instructions** guide generation.
- **CI pipeline** blocks violations.

In practice, **tests are the strongest link between spec and code**. Documentation can be ignored, but a failing test forces the specification to be respected.
